He did not move for a long moment. He simply stood there, a tall, formidable figure who seemed to fill the small room, his presence a tangible force. She braced herself, expecting a further argument, another command, but instead he gave a slight, formal bow of his head.

"As you wish," he said. "For now. But think on what I have said. Pride is a cold comfort on a winter's night." He turned and walked to the door, his steps measured and sure. With his hand on the latch, he paused and looked back at her. "My sister's invitation stands, regardless of your answer to my other proposition. The address is on the card I left. And then he was gone. The closing of the front door was a soft, definitive sound. Helen stood motionless in the centre of the room, listening to the sound of his motor-car starting and then fading into the distance. Silence descended upon Blackwood, a silence heavier and more profound than any she had ever known. She sank into a chair, her legs suddenly refusing to support her.

He intended to marry her. The words echoed in her mind, not with the sweetness of a lover's plea, but with the force of a royal decree. And the most terrifying part, the part she scarcely dared to admit to her own soul, was the treacherous leap her heart had given. The hope. The sudden, dazzling vision of a life where she was not alone, where the crushing weight was lifted, where she might simply rest. It was a vision so beautiful, so seductive, that it felt like a mortal sin.

She pressed her cold hands to her burning cheeks. It was the weakness of the body, she told herself. She was tired, overwrought. Any port in a storm. But he was not a port; he was a tidal wave, threatening to sweep away the very foundations of her world, of herself. To yield to him would be to cease to be Helen Armstrong, mistress of Blackwood; she would become merely Mrs. Davies, an elegant chattel whose life was arranged for her comfort. The thought was an abomination.

She rose and began to pace the room, the familiar squeak of a loose floorboard a small, comforting reality in the midst of her turmoil. Her eyes fell upon the photograph on the mantelpiece: her father, a stern, bearded man, and beside him, a younger, laughing version of herself, and Robert. Dear, feckless Robert. His smile was so charming, so full of the careless promise that had led them all to ruin. It was for him, for the memory of what Blackwood had been before his disastrous speculations, that she toiled. It was her penance, and his. She had sworn to their father on his deathbed that she would hold the land, that she would restore the family name.

"And you," Mr. Davies had said, "are the woman I intend to marry."

The sheer, masculine certainty of it was an affront. But beneath the affront, a deeper question stirred. Had he said love? No. He had spoken of admiration, of logic, of solutions. It was a contract, a merger. And yet, the way he had looked at her, his gaze so intent, so searching. Had there been something more there? Or was she merely a desperate woman, seeing warmth where there was only the cold fire of ambition and a desire for possession?

The next few days passed in a blur of anxious activity. Helen threw herself into the work of the farm with a desperate, feverish energy, as if by exhausting her body she could quell the turmoil in her mind. She avoided the lane where she might encounter his car; she listened with dread for the sound of its approach. But he did not come. The silence from his direction was as unnerving as his presence had been. It felt like the quiet before a siege.

"It is farm work, Thomas," she corrected him, a little sharply. "And I am the farmer here."

He said no more, but his disapproval was a silent reproach. Later that week, it came to a head. He found her in the barn, trying to repair a piece of machinery with hands that were clumsy and grease-stained. He stood there for a moment, twisting his cap in his hands, before he finally spoke.

"I've come to give my notice, Miss Helen," he said, his voice gruff with misery.

Helen dropped the spanner with a clatter. She felt the blood drain from her face. "Notice? Thomas, what are you talking about? You can't leave. Blackwood is your home."

"It has been," he agreed, his gaze fixed on the dusty floor. "But I'm not the man I was. And this place... it needs more than I can give it. It needs a master, Miss Helen. A proper one." He cleared his throat. "Mr. Davies from the Grange, he's offered me a post. Head gardener. Lighter work, and a cottage for me and the missus for our lifetime. I can't turn it down. I'm sorry."

She stared at him, numb with shock. It was a masterfully cruel stroke. Davies had not attacked her directly; he had simply cut the legs out from under her. Without Thomas, she was truly, impossibly alone.

"I see," she said, her voice a dead thing. "He has bought you. Just as he wishes to buy everything else."

Thomas looked up, his weathered face full of hurt. "It's not like that, miss. He's a hard man, aye, but he's a fair one. He said... he said he was doing it to help you. So's you wouldn't have an old man's wages to worry about, and you'd be forced to get proper help in."

"Proper help," she repeated bitterly. "Yes, I am sure that is what he called it."

She saw Thomas to the gate an hour later, a painful, stilted farewell that felt like the severing of her last tie to the old, safe world. As she watched his retreating figure trudge down the lane, a feeling of utter desolation fell upon her. The farm, silent and vast, seemed to mock her with its needs, its relentless, crushing demands. Pride is a cold comfort. His words came back to her, and for the first time, she felt their truth like a physical blow.

She spent the evening by the fire, not reading, not sewing, but staring into the flames, her mind a blank slate of despair. What was she to do? She could sell. Give up. Admit defeat. The thought was a bitter gall. It would mean breaking her promise to her father. It would mean Robert's disgrace would be the final word on the Armstrong family. And it would mean that Davies had won.

A storm broke during the night, a wild autumn gale that lashed the old house with wind and rain. The windows rattled in their frames, and the wind howled in the chimney like a soul in torment. Helen lay awake, listening to the fury of the elements, a strange sense of kinship with the storm's wildness filling her. Her heart leaped into her throat. The old oak. The one that stood by the river bank, its roots already weakened by the water's slow erosion. And the fence beneath it. The rain was a solid, driving sheet, cold and merciless. Bending her head against the gale, a lantern swinging wildly in her hand, she fought her way towards the lower pasture.

The scene was even worse than she had imagined. The giant oak lay like a fallen titan, its massive branches stretched across the field. It had taken a huge section of the fence with it, leaving a gaping hole. The heifers, terrified by the storm, were huddled at the far end of the field, but it would only be a matter of time before one of them panicked and made for the gap, and the deadly rush of the river beyond.

She had to block the gap. But how? She was one woman, against the storm, against the weight of fallen timber. She tried to drag a smaller fallen branch into the space, but it was waterlogged and heavy, and the wind fought her every step. Her lantern blew out, plunging her into a terrifying, windswept darkness. Sobbing with frustration and despair, she sank to her knees in the mud. It was over. She was beaten.

A figure, tall and broad in a heavy coat, vaulted the gate and strode towards her. She did not need to see his face to know who it was. Her heart hammered against her ribs, a wild drumbeat of dread and a desperate, shameful relief.

He reached her side, the beam of his lamp falling on her pathetic, mud-soaked figure. He said nothing, simply played the light over the downed tree, the broken fence, the terrified cattle. His assessment was swift and silent.

"Stay here," he commanded, his voice easily carrying over the wind. "Don't move."

He turned and strode back towards the gate, shouting an order she could not quite hear. A few minutes later, the headlights of his motor-car were joined by those of a larger vehicle, a lorry. Two men jumped out, and under Davies's terse directions, they began to unload ropes, stakes, and a heavy roll of wire fencing.

He came back to her. "My car is at the gate. Go and get in it. You will catch your death out here."

"No," she said, her teeth chattering so hard she could barely form the word. "They are my cattle. This is my responsibility."

He looked down at her for a long, silent moment. She expected an explosion of anger, a sharp command. Instead, he reached down and took her arm, pulling her to her feet. His grip was firm, but not rough.

"Very well," he said, his voice close to her ear. "Then hold the lamp. And try not to get in the way."

For the next two hours, she was a small, silent part of a whirlwind of disciplined activity. Davies was everywhere at once, directing his men, his voice calm and authoritative, never raised but always obeyed. He worked alongside them, his fine coat discarded, his shoulders straining as he helped haul a massive limb out of the way. He seemed a creature of the storm himself, elemental and untiring. Helen, holding the lamp, felt her own smallness, her own utter inadequacy. She had tried to fight the storm and been broken by it. He had arrived and simply tamed it.

At last, a makeshift but sturdy barrier was in place. The heifers were secure. The men from the lorry, with a nod from Davies, packed their tools and left. They were alone again in the receding storm, the rain now just a soft drizzle.

"It is done," he said, turning to her. He was soaked to the skin, his hair plastered to his forehead, mud caking his boots and trousers. He looked less like the master of the Grange and more like a common labourer, and yet, somehow, he had never seemed more formidable.

"Thank you," she said, the words ridiculously inadequate. "I don't know how I can ever repay you."

"There is no need for repayment," he said. He took the lamp from her unresisting hand. "Now, I am taking you back to the house. You need to get out of these wet clothes."

They walked back in silence. He did not touch her, but she was as aware of him as if he had held her in his arms. In the kitchen, the fire she had banked was still glowing. He knelt and threw on a few small logs, coaxing it back to life.

"Go and change," he said, without looking at her. "I will make some tea."

It was a command, but this time she did not resent it. She was too tired, too cold, too utterly spent to argue. When she came back downstairs, wrapped in a thick woollen dressing-gown, her hair unbound and towel-dried, she found two mugs of steaming tea on the kitchen table. He was standing by the window, looking out at the grey dawn.

He turned as she entered. His eyes took in her altered appearance, the loose robe, the damp hair clinging to her shoulders. A look she could not decipher passed over his face.

"You should not have gone out," he said, his voice rough. "It was a fool's errand. You could have been killed."

"They would have drowned," she said simply.

"Better the cattle than you," he retorted. He gestured to the table. "Sit down and drink your tea before it gets cold."

She obeyed, her hands wrapping around the warm mug as if it were a lifeline. He sat opposite her, his own tea untouched. The silence stretched, filled only by the crackle of the fire and the drip of water from the eaves.

"Why were you out?" she asked at last. "How did you know?"

"I was watching the storm from my study," he said. "I saw the lights in your house go on and off. Then I saw your lantern heading for the pasture. I guessed the rest."

So he had been watching her. The thought sent a strange shiver through her, not of fear, but of something else entirely.

"You see," he said, his voice quiet again, "you cannot manage this alone. The elements are against you. The world is against you. It is not a disgrace to admit it. It is merely a fact."

She looked down into her mug, unable to meet his eyes. "What do you want from me, Mr. Davies?" she asked, her voice barely a whisper.

He reached across the table and tilted her chin up with one finger, forcing her to look at him. His eyes were very dark, the searching intensity back in them, but softened now with a different light.

"I have already told you," he said, his voice a low gravelly murmur that seemed to resonate in her very bones. "But perhaps I was not clear enough. It is not a business transaction, Helen. It is not about logic, or acres, or a crumbling house. Though God knows, I will fix all of that." He paused, and his thumb moved gently, tracing the line of her jaw. "When I saw you kneeling in the mud out there, so small and defiant, with the whole world coming down around you, I did not think of logic. I thought my heart would stop." He drew a breath. "I want to take care of you. I want to stand between you and the storm. And I want you to be my wife. Is that clear enough now?"

She stared at him, her lips parted, the world tilting on its axis for the second time in a week. The terror was still there, a faint, trembling shadow, but the hope, a brilliant, blinding sun, was rising to consume it. He had spoken not of admiration, but of his heart. And in that moment, all her pride, all her defences, all her lonely, bitter resolves, crumbled into dust.
